content.title: About
content.content: Octopus is a marine mollusk belonging to the class Cephalopoda, found in warm seas worldwide. Its meat is tender, mildly sweet, and carries a distinct oceanic flavor. It is used in many cuisines, often sliced into rings, served in sushi, salads, or stewed dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Octopuses have eight arms, each lined with suction cups that allow them to grasp and sense their environment.
They are highly intelligent, capable of solving puzzles, using tools, and remembering maze routes.
Most species can change skin color and texture for camouflage.
Octopuses can regenerate lost arms within a few weeks.
In Japan octopus is a delicacy, while in the Mediterranean it is commonly prepared in stews.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Octopus meat provides about 15 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, making it an excellent protein source.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: It contains very little saturated fat, suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Octopus is rich in iron, zinc, magnesium, and selenium, supporting immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: A modest amount of omega‑3 contributes to heart health and reduces inflammation.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to octopus, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Natural toxins
items.content: Certain wild species (e.g., blue‑ringed octopus) contain toxins, but commercially sold varieties are generally safe.

items.title: Food parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked seafood can harbor parasites; cooking octopus to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C is recommended.

items.title: High sodium in canned forms
items.content: Canned octopus often contains added salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Octopus is commonly boiled, grilled, baked, or steamed. It is sliced into rings for salads, sushi, paella, and risotto. Tenderizing by gently beating the meat before cooking improves texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh octopus should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 1‑2 days. Frozen octopus retains quality for up to 6 months at –18 °C. Thaw in the fridge and rinse thoroughly before preparation.
